summary:
Aceh stands under Indonesia's national framework, and the two layers compound each other. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level morality provisions.

Aceh is the only province in the country operating a codified religious criminal law of its own, the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014). It criminalises same-sex conduct under the headings liwath and musahaqah and criminalises close proximity as khalwat. Sentences are imposed by Islamic Shariah courts and policed by the Wilayatul Hisbah religious force alongside secular Satpol PP units, and the punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

The penalty scale runs to 100 strokes for morality offences, and public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences. In August 2025 a Sharia court convicted two men of hugging and kissing and sentenced each to 80 strokes; they were caned in a public park before around 100 spectators, and eight more people were caned the same day. CBS News and AP reported the caning on 26 August 2025. In February 2025 two men were publicly caned in Aceh for a same-sex relationship.

The Qanun does not name transgender people, but enforcement reaches them. A February 2025 round-up at a boarding house detained a waria and a gay student who faced up to 100 strokes under the province's provisions.

A trans visitor has died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Venue enforcement is documented as well. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.
tangentialFactors:
Indonesia is not alone at provincial level: the Human Dignity Trust profile places Aceh alongside South Sumatra as the two provinces criminalising same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. South Sumatra does not operate a religious criminal code of the kind Aceh does, so the caning regime and the religious police are the Aceh-specific features rather than a national norm.

Indonesia-wide survey data collected by the UNSW Human Rights Research Centre finds that transgender women experience the highest rates of violence of any LGBTIQ group in the country, together with high levels of measured social hostility. That national pattern is the backdrop to Aceh's enforcement, and the province's public-caning practice sits inside it rather than beside it.

The August 2026 reporting connecting vigilante attacks on transgender women to the October 2025 presidential decree describes a shift in which hostile attitudes already present in public opinion acquire the backing of official defence doctrine. Commentators quoted by ABC News characterise the regulation as moving hostile rhetoric into national defence policy.

Raids on private gatherings are not confined to Aceh. The 22 June 2025 operation near Bogor, in which 75 people were arrested from a rented villa, shows that gatherings identified as gay are liable to be broken up by secular police elsewhere in Indonesia as well.
localsOnly:
Residents of Aceh are policed for these offences by two forces working in parallel: the Wilayatul Hisbah religious police and the secular Satpol PP public order units, with the Islamic Shariah courts handing down the sentences. The Feb 2025 boarding-house round-up targeted people in local accommodation, and the students detained in it were residents rather than visitors.

Local scholarship treats the waria population as a matter of law-enforcement administration. "The Increasing Number of Waria in Banda Aceh: Between Social Challenges and Law Enforcement", by scholars at UIN Ar-Raniry and published in QURU: Journal of Family Law and Culture (doi 10.59698/quru.v3i1.405), analyses the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens, with keywords covering law enforcement, waria, Aceh, Islamic law and the Qanun.

The public-canelling sentences are served locally and observed locally: the August 2025 caning in a park drew roughly 100 spectators, and eight other people were punished the same day in the same setting.
outOfScopeNotes:
The January 2018 detention of twelve trans women is documented in national material, and no Aceh-specific source in the current inventory confirms where it occurred or how it was resolved. The point is recorded as unresolved rather than attributed to Aceh.

The inventory does not resolve whether the Qanun on jinayat has been applied to a foreign visitor, or whether any of the caning sentences documented here involved a non-Indonesian national. The parent framework states that Aceh's punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; specific cases involving foreign nationals are not sourced.

Whether Aceh's provisions have ever been used against a person on the basis of gender identity, as distinct from sexual conduct, is not documented here. The Qanun does not name transgender people, and the trans-person enforcement described in the sources consists of detentions and round-ups rather than a named charge.
